docs.title: pq
docs.text:
Postgres-backed job queue for Python with fork-based worker isolation.

If you already run Postgres, you don't need Redis or RabbitMQ to process background jobs. pq uses SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED to turn your existing database into a reliable task queue. Enqueue in the same transaction as your writes, and process tasks in isolated child processes that can't crash your worker.

from pq import PQ

pq = PQ("postgresql://localhost/mydb")
pq.run_db_migrations()

def send_email(to: str, subject: str) -> None:
    ...

pq.enqueue(send_email, to="user@example.com", subject="Hello")
pq.run_worker()

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
uv add python-pq

Or with pip:

pip install python-pq

Requires PostgreSQL and Python 3.13+.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Fork isolation -- Each task runs in a forked child process. If it OOMs, segfaults, or crashes, the worker keeps running. Each child gets a fresh connection pool and opens its own database connections.
  • No extra infrastructure -- Uses your existing Postgres. No broker to deploy, monitor, or lose data.
  • Transactional enqueueing -- Enqueue tasks in the same database transaction as your writes. If the transaction rolls back, the task is never created.
  • Periodic tasks -- Schedule with intervals (timedelta) or cron expressions. Control overlap, pause/resume without deleting.
  • Priority queues -- Five levels from BATCH (0) to CRITICAL (100). Dedicate workers to specific priority tiers.
  • Lifecycle hooks -- Run pre_execute / post_execute code in the forked child, safe for fork-unsafe libraries like OpenTelemetry.

docs.title: Enqueueing
docs.text:
Pass any importable function with its arguments:

def greet(name: str) -> None:
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

pq.enqueue(greet, name="World")
pq.enqueue(greet, "World")  # Positional args work too

docs.title: Delayed execution
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, UTC

pq.enqueue(greet, "World", run_at=datetime.now(UTC) + timedelta(hours=1))

docs.title: Priority
docs.text:
from pq import Priority

pq.enqueue(task, priority=Priority.CRITICAL)  # 100 - runs first
pq.enqueue(task, priority=Priority.HIGH)      # 75
pq.enqueue(task, priority=Priority.NORMAL)    # 50 (default)
pq.enqueue(task, priority=Priority.LOW)       # 25
pq.enqueue(task, priority=Priority.BATCH)     # 0 - runs last

docs.title: Cancellation
docs.text:
task_id = pq.enqueue(my_task)
pq.cancel(task_id)  # True if the task was deleted

cancel() deletes a task that is waiting or finished. A task that is running is left alone and cancel() returns False: pq does not stop a run in progress.

docs.title: Client IDs
docs.text:
Use client_id for idempotency and lookups:

pq.enqueue(process_order, order_id=123, client_id="order-123")

task = pq.get_task_by_client_id("order-123")
# Duplicate client_id raises IntegrityError

docs.title: Upsert
docs.text:
Insert or update a task by client_id. Useful for debouncing -- only the latest version runs:

pq.upsert(send_email, to="a@b.com", client_id="welcome-email")

# Second call updates the existing task (resets to PENDING)
pq.upsert(send_email, to="new@b.com", client_id="welcome-email")

If the task is running, the new version is queued and runs after the current run ends, so one client_id does not run twice at the same time. This lets a task schedule its own continuation:

def backfill(offset: int) -> None:
    more = process_rows(offset, limit=1000)
    if more:
        with PQ(DATABASE_URL) as client:
            # Runs after this run ends, never next to it
            client.upsert(backfill, offset=offset + 1000, client_id="backfill")

If the worker running the task dies, the queued version runs once another worker notices, about a minute later (see Dead workers).

For a batch, upsert_many() takes a list of Upsert items and writes them in one transaction:

from pq import Upsert

pq.upsert_many(
    [Upsert(task=send_email, kwargs={"to": to}, client_id=f"welcome-{to}") for to in emails]
)

docs.title: Intervals
docs.text:
from datetime import timedelta

def heartbeat() -> None:
    print("alive")

pq.schedule(heartbeat, run_every=timedelta(minutes=5))

Call schedule() on every application start: it creates the schedule or updates it. A schedule whose run_every or cron did not change keeps its next run time, so a restart does not run the task again, and a cron time that came due during the restart still runs. A new schedule, one whose timing changed, and one that was inactive first run right away (run_every) or at the next cron time.

docs.title: Cron expressions
docs.text: pq.schedule(weekly_report, cron="0 9 * * 1")  # Monday 9am

docs.title: With arguments
docs.text: pq.schedule(report, run_every=timedelta(hours=1), report_type="hourly")

docs.title: Overlap control
docs.text:
By default, periodic tasks don't overlap -- if an instance is still running when the next tick arrives, the tick is skipped:

# Default: max_concurrent=1, no overlap
pq.schedule(sync_inventory, run_every=timedelta(minutes=5))

# Allow unlimited concurrency
pq.schedule(fast_task, run_every=timedelta(seconds=30), max_concurrent=None)

docs.title: Pausing and resuming
docs.text:
# Pause -- task stays in the database but won't run
pq.schedule(sync_inventory, run_every=timedelta(minutes=5), active=False)

# Resume
pq.schedule(sync_inventory, run_every=timedelta(minutes=5), active=True)

docs.title: Multiple schedules
docs.text:
Use key to register the same function with different configurations:

pq.schedule(sync_data, run_every=timedelta(hours=1), key="us", region="us")
pq.schedule(sync_data, run_every=timedelta(hours=2), key="eu", region="eu")

pq.unschedule(sync_data, key="us")

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
pq.run_worker(poll_interval=1.0)           # Run forever
processed = pq.run_worker_once()            # Process single task (for testing)

run_worker_once() is one claim and one run. It has no heartbeat, cleanup, stale reaper or signal handling; a program that loops over it calls pq.reap_stale_tasks() itself.

docs.title: Stopping
docs.text:
On SIGTERM or SIGINT the worker stops claiming, waits up to drain_timeout seconds (default 20) for the tasks in flight, then kills what is still running and marks it failed. pq.stop_worker() starts the same shutdown from code. A worker that runs outside the main thread gets no signals, so there it is the only way:

thread = threading.Thread(target=pq.run_worker)
thread.start()
...
pq.stop_worker()
thread.join()

stop_worker() also works before the worker has got going: the next run_worker in the process then stops as soon as it starts.

docs.title: Failed tasks
docs.text:
A failed task has status == TaskStatus.FAILED, the text of the failure in error, and its cause in failure_kind:

FailureKind Cause ERROR The task raised, or its process exited with an error TIMEOUT It ran past its max runtime OOM Its process was killed from outside with SIGKILL, most likely for memory KILLED Its process was ended by another signal SHUTDOWN The worker's drain ran out and killed it WORKER_LOST Its worker stopped sending heartbeats STALE It was still marked running past its stale window

pq does not retry. To run tasks again that a deploy interrupted, select them by cause:

from pq import FailureKind

for task in pq.list_failed():
    if task.failure_kind == FailureKind.SHUTDOWN:
        ...

docs.title: Dead workers
docs.text:
Each worker keeps a row in pq_workers and extends a lease there every 15 seconds. When a worker dies without shutting down (the machine is lost, the process is killed), its lease runs out after 60 seconds. Any other worker then fails the tasks it was running with FailureKind.WORKER_LOST, or re-queues them if an upsert() had queued a new version.

On Linux the kernel kills a task's process when its worker dies, so a task marked this way is not running any more. On other systems it can run on to its end.

A worker that is alive but cut off from the database for more than 60 seconds is taken for dead as well, by the workers that can reach it. Its tasks keep running. If one of them finishes and its row is still failed as WORKER_LOST, its real result replaces that. If your application re-queued the row in between, the task has run twice.

The stale reaper (stale_task_timeout, default 1 hour) remains for what the heartbeat cannot see: a task run by run_worker_once(), or a run whose result could not be written. A task counts as stale once it has been running for longer than stale_task_timeout and twice the max runtime of its run.

docs.title: Timeout
docs.text:
Kill tasks that run too long:

pq.run_worker(max_runtime=300)  # 5 minute timeout per task

The task's process stops itself at max_runtime. If it cannot (it is blocked in native code, or the task changed its own SIGALRM handling), the worker kills it 10 seconds later, with anything it started. A TimeoutError raised by the task itself is an ordinary failure, with its traceback.

docs.title: Priority-dedicated workers
docs.text:
Reserve workers for high-priority tasks:

from pq import Priority

# This worker only processes CRITICAL and HIGH
pq.run_worker(priorities={Priority.CRITICAL, Priority.HIGH})

docs.title: Lifecycle hooks
docs.text:
Run code before/after each task in the forked child process:

from pq import PQ, Task, Periodic

def setup_tracing(task: Task | Periodic) -> None:
    print(f"Starting: {task.name}")

def flush_tracing(task: Task | Periodic, error: Exception | None) -> None:
    if error:
        print(f"Failed: {error}")

pq.run_worker(pre_execute=setup_tracing, post_execute=flush_tracing)

Hooks run in the forked child, making them safe for fork-unsafe resources like OpenTelemetry.

The task's result is settled when its function returns. post_execute runs after that and does not change it: if the hook raises, hangs or is killed, a task that finished stays COMPLETED. The hook has until 10 seconds after max_runtime, then the worker kills the process.

docs.title: Calling pq from a task
docs.text:
A task can use your application's PQ instance, for example to enqueue a follow-up task. Each forked child gets a fresh connection pool, opens its own connections, and closes them when the task ends. A child killed by its timeout or by a signal exits without closing them.

If your own code forks (with os.fork() or multiprocessing), fork outside an open pq.session(). A connection checked out at fork time stays shared between the two processes.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
pq uses loguru internally and does not configure the logger on import. This means it inherits whatever logging setup the host application has already established.

If you are running pq as a standalone script and want pq's default log format, call configure_logging() explicitly during startup:

from pq.logging import configure_logging

configure_logging()

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text:
Arguments are serialized automatically:

Type Method JSON-serializable (str, int, list, dict) JSON Pydantic models model_dump(mode="json") → JSON (the task receives a dict) Custom objects, lambdas, NaN, strings with a NUL character dill (pickle)

docs.title: Async tasks
docs.text:
Async handlers work without any changes:

import httpx

async def fetch(url: str) -> None:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        response = await client.get(url)
        print(response.status_code)

pq.enqueue(fetch, "https://example.com")

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
Failed tasks are marked with status FAILED and the error is stored:

for task in pq.list_failed():
    print(f"{task.name}: {task.error}")

pq.clear_failed(before=datetime.now(UTC) - timedelta(days=7))
pq.clear_completed(before=datetime.now(UTC) - timedelta(days=1))

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Every task runs in a forked child process:

Worker (parent)
    |
    +-- fork() -> Child executes task -> exits
    |             (OOM/crash only affects child)
    |
    +-- Continues processing next task

The parent monitors via os.wait4() and detects timeout, OOM (SIGKILL), and signal-based crashes. The child process exits after every task, giving you true memory isolation.

A child shares the worker's memory until it writes to it. The child freezes what it inherited for the garbage collector (gc.freeze()), so a collection in the child does not copy those pages: in a measurement with a 730 MB worker, one collection copied 390 MB without the freeze and 24 MB with it.

One-off tasks and periodic schedules form one queue: the highest priority runs first, and within a priority whichever came due first. A backlog of one-off tasks delays a schedule of the same priority no more than it delays a task that came due at the same time. Give a schedule a higher priority to keep it on time under load.

Multiple workers can run in parallel. Tasks are claimed atomically with PostgreSQL's FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so each task runs exactly once.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
There are good options in this space. pq makes different tradeoffs:

Broker Isolation Use case pq Postgres Fork (process-per-task) Teams already on Postgres who want fewer moving parts Celery Redis/RabbitMQ Per-worker process Large-scale, multi-language, established teams RQ Redis Per-worker process Simple Redis-based queues Dramatiq Redis/RabbitMQ Per-worker process/thread Celery alternative with better defaults ARQ Redis Async (single process) Async-first applications Procrastinate Postgres Async (single process) Async-first, Postgres-backed, Django integration

pq is a good fit when: - You already run Postgres and don't want to add Redis or RabbitMQ - You want transactional enqueueing (enqueue atomically with your writes) - You need true process isolation per task (OOM/crash safety) - You want periodic tasks with overlap control, pause/resume, and cron

pq is not the right choice when: - You need very high throughput (10,000+ jobs/second) -- use a dedicated broker - You need cross-language workers -- Celery or a dedicated queue service is better - You need complex workflows (DAGs, chaining, fan-out) -- look at Temporal or Prefect

docs.title: run_db_migrations()
docs.text:
Run database migrations to latest version.

Call this once at application startup before using the queue. Uses Alembic to apply any pending migrations. Safe to call multiple times - only pending migrations are applied.

Example

pq = PQ("postgresql://localhost/mydb") pq.run_db_migrations()

docs.title: upsert(task, *args, run_at=None, priority=Priority.NORMAL, client_id, max_runtime_seconds=None, **kwargs)
docs.text:
Enqueue a task, updating if client_id already exists.

Behaves like enqueue(), but on conflict for client_id, updates all fields. Status resets to PENDING, attempts to 0, and timestamps are cleared.

If the existing task is RUNNING, it is not changed. The new version is stored on the row and runs after the current run ends (the worker or the stale reaper re-queues the row with it). A second upsert while the row is still RUNNING replaces the stored version, so only the latest one runs. So one client_id does not run twice at the same time. The one exception is a worker that is alive but cut off from the database for longer than its heartbeat lease (pq.worker.WORKER_TIMEOUT_SECONDS): the other workers take it for dead and re-queue the row with the stored version while its run goes on. If the worker running the task died, the stored version runs once another worker notices the missing heartbeat, about a minute later.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default task Callable[..., Any]

Callable function to execute.

required *args Any

Positional arguments to pass to the handler.

() run_at datetime | None

When to run the task. Defaults to now.

None priority Priority

Task priority. Higher = higher priority. Defaults to NORMAL.

NORMAL client_id str

Client-provided identifier. Required for conflict resolution.

required max_runtime_seconds float | None

Per-task wall-clock cap in seconds. See enqueue for details. None (the default) leaves the worker's own configured max_runtime_seconds in effect.

None **kwargs Any

Keyword arguments to pass to the handler.

{}

Returns:

Type Description int

Task ID.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If task is a lambda, closure, or cannot be imported, or if max_runtime_seconds is not None and <= 0.

docs.title: upsert_many(upserts)
docs.text:
Upsert several tasks in one transaction.

Each item behaves like upsert() with the same arguments, so a RUNNING row gets the new version parked. A repeated client_id ends with its last version. The batch is sent as one multi-row statement per 1000 tasks, against one statement and one commit per upsert() call. Nothing is written if any item fails.

The rows are written in client_id order, so that two batches with overlapping ids lock rows in the same order and cannot deadlock. Each row stays locked until the batch commits: a worker finishing one of these tasks waits for the whole batch. Split very large batches into chunks to keep that wait short.

Returns:

Type Description list[int]

Task IDs, in the order of upserts.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

As upsert(), for the first invalid item.

docs.title: schedule(task, *args, run_every=None, cron=None, priority=Priority.NORMAL, client_id=None, max_concurrent=1, key='', active=True, max_runtime_seconds=None, **kwargs)
docs.text:
Schedule a periodic task.

If a periodic task with this function and key already exists, it is updated. Its next run stays where it was unless run_every or cron changed, so calling this on every application start does not run the task each time. A new schedule, one whose timing changed, and one that was inactive first run now (run_every) or at the next cron time. Either run_every or cron must be provided, but not both.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default task Callable[..., Any]

Callable function to execute.

required *args Any

Positional arguments to pass to the handler.

() run_every timedelta | None

Interval between executions (e.g., timedelta(hours=1)).

None cron str | croniter | None

Cron expression string (e.g., "0 9 * * 1") or croniter object.

None priority Priority

Task priority. Higher = higher priority. Defaults to NORMAL.

NORMAL client_id str | None

Optional client-provided identifier. Must be unique if provided.

None max_concurrent int | None

Maximum concurrent executions. Default 1 (no overlap). Set to None for unlimited concurrency. Values > 1 are reserved for future use and raise ValueError.

1 key str

Discriminator for multiple schedules of the same function. Defaults to "" (empty string).

'' active bool

Whether the task is active. Inactive tasks are not executed. Defaults to True.

True max_runtime_seconds float | None

Per-execution wall-clock cap in seconds. When None (the common case), each execution uses the worker's configured default. When set, this schedule's executions get the supplied ceiling, and the locked_until window (used when max_concurrent is in effect) is extended to match so the lock doesn't expire while the execution is legitimately still running. Periodic tasks are not subject to the stale-task reaper, so this knob is purely about the wall-clock cap.

None **kwargs Any

Keyword arguments to pass to the handler.

{}

Returns:

Type Description int

Periodic task ID.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If neither run_every nor cron is provided, or if both are.

ValueError

If cron expression is invalid.

ValueError

If max_concurrent is greater than 1.

ValueError

If task is a lambda, closure, or cannot be imported.

ValueError

If max_runtime_seconds is not None and <= 0.

IntegrityError

If client_id already exists.

docs.title: cancel(task_id)
docs.text:
Cancel a one-off task by ID: delete it, unless it is running.

A RUNNING task is left alone and False is returned. pq does not stop a run in progress, and deleting its row would only hide it: the run would go on, and a task enqueued again under the same client_id would run next to it. A version that an upsert() parked on the running row stays parked as well.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default task_id int

Task ID.

required

Returns:

Type Description bool

True if the task was found and deleted. False if there is no

bool

such task, or it is running.

docs.title: run_worker(*, concurrency=1, poll_interval=1.0, max_runtime=30 * 60, priorities=None, retention_days=7, cleanup_interval=3600, stale_task_timeout=timedelta(hours=1), drain_timeout=20.0, pre_execute=None, post_execute=None)
docs.text:
Run the worker loop (blocking). Same as pq.worker.run_worker, which documents every argument and the shutdown in full.

Each task executes in a forked child process for memory isolation.

On SIGTERM or SIGINT the worker stops claiming new tasks, waits up to drain_timeout seconds for in-flight tasks to finish, then kills any still-running task and marks its row FAILED with an explicit shutdown error. Interrupted tasks are not re-queued, unless an upsert() stored a new version while they ran: then the row is re-queued with that version.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default concurrency int

Maximum number of tasks to process simultaneously. Default: 1 (sequential processing).

1 poll_interval float

Seconds to sleep between polls when idle.

1.0 max_runtime float

Maximum execution time per task in seconds. Default: 30 min.

30 * 60 priorities Set[Priority] | None

If set, only process tasks with these priority levels. Use this to dedicate workers to specific priority tiers.

None retention_days int

Days to keep completed/failed tasks. Default: 7. 0 disables the cleanup.

7 cleanup_interval float

Seconds between cleanup runs. Default: 1 hour.

3600 stale_task_timeout timedelta | None

Fail RUNNING tasks older than this (see reap_stale_tasks). Default: 1 hour. None disables it.

timedelta(hours=1) drain_timeout float

Seconds to wait for in-flight tasks on SIGTERM/SIGINT. Default: 20. Set below the orchestrator's termination grace period. 0 skips the wait: in-flight tasks are killed as soon as the shutdown is noticed.

20.0 pre_execute PreExecuteHook | None

Called in the forked child before the task runs.

None post_execute PostExecuteHook | None

Called in the forked child after the task ran, with the exception it raised or None.

None

docs.title: stop_worker()
docs.text: Ask the worker running in this process to drain and stop, the way SIGTERM does. Safe to call from any thread, and the only way to stop a worker that runs outside the main thread. See pq.worker.stop_worker.

docs.title: reap_stale_tasks(threshold)
docs.text:
Mark stale RUNNING tasks as FAILED, or re-queue them.

A RUNNING row can outlive its run: the worker died without a heartbeat to miss (run_worker_once has none), or the run ended and its result could not be written. This method finds those rows by their age and fails them (FailureKind.STALE).

A stale row that holds a version parked by upsert() (see Task.requeue) is re-queued as PENDING with that version instead of being failed, so the parked version is not lost.

A row is stale when it has been RUNNING for longer than max(threshold, 2 * max runtime of its run). The max runtime of the run is what its claim wrote to the row: the task's own max_runtime_seconds, or the default of the worker that claimed it. So a reaper with a short window does not fail the runs of a worker with a longer max runtime. A row claimed by a version of pq that did not record this falls back to the task's own max_runtime_seconds, and then to threshold.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default threshold timedelta

The shortest stale window. A task is stale when started_at + effective_threshold < now().

required

Returns:

Type Description int

Number of tasks reaped (failed plus re-queued).

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: pq raises no exceptions of its own for a task that fails: the outcome is on the task (status, error, failure_kind). pq.TaskTimeoutError and the other exception classes in pq.worker were never raised. They are deprecated and will be removed.

docs.title: PQ Client
docs.text:
The main interface for your application:

from pq import PQ

pq = PQ("postgresql://localhost/mydb")

# Enqueue one-off tasks
pq.enqueue(send_email, to="user@example.com")

# Schedule recurring tasks
pq.schedule(cleanup, run_every=timedelta(hours=1))

docs.title: PostgreSQL Tables
docs.text:
pq_tasks - One-off tasks:

Column Purpose name Function path (e.g., myapp.tasks:send_email) payload JSONB with serialized args/kwargs priority 0-100, higher runs first status pending → running → completed/failed run_at Scheduled execution time error Error message if failed failure_kind Why it failed: error, timeout, oom, killed, shutdown, worker_lost or stale requeue JSONB with the next version, stored by an upsert() that arrived while the task was running. Applied when the run ends worker_id The pq_workers row of the worker running it. Set by the claim, cleared when the run ends worker_claimed_at The started_at of the claim that wrote worker_id. The orphan check ignores a worker_id that an earlier claim left on the row claimed_max_runtime_seconds The max runtime of the run in progress: the task's own, or the default of the worker that claimed it

pq_periodic - Recurring schedules:

Column Purpose name Function path (unique with key) key Discriminator for multiple schedules of the same function (default "") payload JSONB with serialized args/kwargs priority 0-100, higher runs first run_every Interval (e.g., 1 hour) cron Cron expression (e.g., 0 9 * * 1) active Whether the task is executed (default true) next_run Next scheduled execution

pq_workers - Running workers:

Column Purpose hostname, pid Where the worker runs started_at When it started expires_at End of its heartbeat lease. The worker moves it 60 s ahead every 15 s

docs.title: Fork Isolation
docs.text:
Every task runs in an isolated child process:

flowchart LR
    subgraph parent["Worker (Parent)"]
        poll["Poll for task"]
        fork["fork()"]
        wait["wait4()"]
        update["Update status"]
    end

    subgraph child["Child Process"]
        setup["Set timeout"]
        pre["pre_execute()"]
        exec["Execute handler"]
        report["Report outcome"]
        post["post_execute()"]
        exit["exit()"]
    end

    poll --> fork
    fork --> setup
    setup --> pre
    pre --> exec
    exec --> report
    report --> post
    post --> exit
    report -.->|"pipe"| wait
    exit -.->|"exit code"| wait
    wait --> update
    update --> poll

When the handler returns or raises, the child writes the outcome to a pipe, before post_execute runs. That outcome is the task's result, however the process ends afterwards. If the child wrote nothing, the handler did not get to its end, and the way the process ended decides:

What the worker sees Result failure_kind Pipe: handler returned COMPLETED Pipe: error report FAILED with the traceback error Exit code 124 (the child stopped itself), or the worker's SIGKILL 10 s after max_runtime FAILED with timeout timeout The worker's SIGKILL at the end of its drain FAILED with shutdown error shutdown SIGKILL from outside (signal 9) FAILED with OOM oom Other signals FAILED with signal killed

Benefits:

  • Memory isolation - Child OOM doesn't crash worker
  • Crash isolation - Segfaults only kill the child
  • Clean state - Each task starts fresh
  • Hook safety - Lifecycle hooks run in the child, safe for fork-unsafe resources

docs.title: Lifecycle Hooks
docs.text:
Optional pre_execute and post_execute hooks run in the forked child:

from pq import Task, Periodic

def pre_execute(task: Task | Periodic) -> None:
    # Initialize fork-unsafe resources (OTel, DB connections)
    pass

def post_execute(task: Task | Periodic, error: Exception | None) -> None:
    # Cleanup/flush (OTel traces, etc.)
    pass

pq.run_worker(pre_execute=pre_execute, post_execute=post_execute)

This is essential for OpenTelemetry and similar libraries that don't survive fork().

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
Multiple workers safely process tasks in parallel using PostgreSQL's FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED:

flowchart LR
    subgraph workers["Workers"]
        w1["Worker 1"]
        w2["Worker 2"]
        w3["Worker 3"]
    end

    subgraph db["pq_tasks"]
        t1["Task A 🔒 W1"]
        t2["Task B 🔒 W2"]
        t3["Task C 🔒 W3"]
        t4["Task D ⏳"]
        t5["Task E ⏳"]
    end

    w1 -.-> t1
    w2 -.-> t2
    w3 -.-> t3
UPDATE pq_tasks
SET status = 'RUNNING', started_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1,
    worker_id = :worker_id, worker_claimed_at = now(),
    claimed_max_runtime_seconds = coalesce(max_runtime_seconds, :worker_max_runtime)
WHERE id = (
    SELECT id FROM pq_tasks
    WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND run_at <= now()
    ORDER BY priority DESC, run_at
    LIMIT 1
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
RETURNING *;
  • FOR UPDATE locks the selected row
  • SKIP LOCKED skips rows locked by other workers
  • Each task runs exactly once
  • The partial index ix_pq_tasks_pending holds the pending rows in this order, so a claim reads its first entry however long the backlog is

One-off tasks and periodic schedules form one queue: priority first, then the time they came due. Before the claim above, the worker reads the first due schedule. If there is one, the task is claimed only if it goes before it; otherwise the schedule is claimed, in a transaction that locks it and advances it to its next run.

Claiming a task, recording its result and enqueuing are one statement each, sent in autocommit: no BEGIN and COMMIT round trips. A poll that finds nothing costs three statements (connection check, read of the schedules, claim), a processed task five, an enqueue two. The heartbeat adds a connection check and up to two statements per worker every 15 seconds.

docs.title: Priority System
docs.text:
Tasks are processed in priority order (higher first):

Priority Value Use Case CRITICAL 100 User-facing, time-sensitive HIGH 75 Important but less urgent NORMAL 50 Default LOW 25 Background work BATCH 0 Bulk operations

Dedicated workers can handle specific priorities:

# High-priority worker
pq.run_worker(priorities={Priority.CRITICAL, Priority.HIGH})

# Batch worker
pq.run_worker(priorities={Priority.BATCH})

docs.title: Task Lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    state "RUNNING" as R
    state "RUNNING, new version parked" as RP
    [*] --> PENDING: enqueue() or upsert()
    PENDING --> PENDING: upsert() overwrites
    PENDING --> R: worker claims
    R --> RP: upsert() parks a version
    RP --> RP: upsert() replaces it
    R --> COMPLETED: handler returned
    R --> FAILED: run failed, worker lost, or stale
    RP --> PENDING: run ends, worker lost, or stale
    COMPLETED --> PENDING: upsert()
    FAILED --> PENDING: upsert()
    FAILED --> COMPLETED: late result after WORKER_LOST
    PENDING --> [*]: cancel()
    COMPLETED --> [*]: cancel() or cleanup
    FAILED --> [*]: cancel() or cleanup

Each transition is one SQL statement whose WHERE clause is its guard. cancel() does not match a RUNNING row.

upsert() on a RUNNING task does not change the run in progress. It stores the new version in requeue. When the run ends (success, failure, timeout, shutdown, or a reap), the row goes back to PENDING with that version instead of COMPLETED or FAILED. So one client_id does not run twice at the same time.

The worker records the end of a run only if the row still belongs to that run: it is RUNNING with the started_at of the run's claim. A run that ends after its row was reaped and claimed again leaves the row alone.

docs.title: Rows left RUNNING
docs.text:
A row can stay RUNNING with no run behind it. Two checks find such rows, and both fail the row or, if a version is parked, re-queue it:

  • Worker lost. Each worker holds a lease in pq_workers and renews it every 15 s. A RUNNING row whose worker_id (written by its current claim) points at a lease that ran out (60 s without a renewal), or at no row, is orphaned. Every worker runs this check after each of its own heartbeats, once it has itself renewed on time for a whole lease. That wait matters after a database outage: every lease has run out then, and the live workers have to renew before anyone judges them. On Linux a task's process is killed by the kernel when its worker dies (PR_SET_PDEATHSIG), so an orphaned row has no process behind it.
  • Stale. A row that has been RUNNING for longer than stale_task_timeout (default 1 hour) and twice its claimed_max_runtime_seconds. This covers rows without a worker id (run_worker_once) and runs whose result could not be written.

A worker that was cut off from the database and comes back may find its tasks failed as worker_lost while they ran. When such a run ends, its result replaces the verdict, unless the row was re-queued in the meantime.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: How pq compares to other Python task queues.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Broker Worker model Periodic tasks Process isolation pq Postgres Fork per task Interval + cron Yes (fork) Celery Redis / RabbitMQ Process pool Beat scheduler Per worker RQ Redis Process per worker rq-scheduler Per worker Dramatiq Redis / RabbitMQ Thread / process pool APScheduler Per worker ARQ Redis Async event loop Built-in cron No Procrastinate Postgres Async event loop Built-in No

docs.title: Why Postgres as a broker?
docs.text:
Most task queues require a separate message broker (Redis, RabbitMQ). If your application already uses Postgres, adding another stateful service means:

  • Another thing to deploy, monitor, back up, and keep running
  • Another failure mode (broker goes down, queue is lost)
  • No transactional guarantees between your writes and your enqueues

With a Postgres-backed queue, you can enqueue a task in the same transaction as your database write. If the transaction rolls back, the task is never created. No two-phase commit, no outbox pattern.

The tradeoff is throughput. Postgres is not optimized for high-frequency polling. If you need 10,000+ jobs per second, use a dedicated broker. For most applications processing hundreds or low thousands of jobs per second, Postgres handles it well.

docs.title: pq vs Celery
docs.text:
Celery is the most widely used Python task queue. It's battle-tested and feature-rich.

Choose Celery when:

  • You need very high throughput
  • You need cross-language workers (Celery has Node.js, Go clients)
  • You need complex workflows (chains, chords, groups)
  • Your team already knows Celery

Choose pq when:

  • You don't want to run Redis or RabbitMQ
  • You want true process isolation per task (not per worker)
  • You want transactional enqueueing
  • You prefer a smaller API surface

docs.title: pq vs RQ (Redis Queue)
docs.text:
RQ is a simple Redis-based queue. It's easy to get started with.

Choose RQ when:

  • You already run Redis
  • You want a minimal, well-known library

Choose pq when:

  • You don't want to add Redis to your stack
  • You need periodic tasks with overlap control
  • You want fork isolation per task (RQ isolates per worker, not per task)

docs.title: pq vs Procrastinate
docs.text:
Procrastinate is the closest alternative -- it's also Postgres-backed and well-designed.

Choose Procrastinate when:

  • You want async-first workers (Procrastinate runs tasks in an async event loop)
  • You use Django (Procrastinate has first-class Django support)
  • You want a more mature, established library

Choose pq when:

  • You want fork-based process isolation (one process per task)
  • You want to pass functions directly without decorating them
  • You don't need Django integration

docs.title: pq vs ARQ
docs.text:
ARQ is an async-first Redis-based queue.

Choose ARQ when:

  • Your application is fully async
  • You already run Redis

Choose pq when:

  • You don't want Redis
  • You need process isolation (ARQ runs everything in one event loop)
  • You need priority queues with dedicated workers

docs.title: Fork isolation
docs.text:
This is pq's key differentiator. Most task queues run tasks in long-lived worker processes. If a task leaks memory, the worker gradually degrades. If a task segfaults or triggers the OOM killer, the worker dies and all in-flight tasks are lost.

pq forks a new child process for every task. The child executes the task and exits. Memory leaks are cleaned up by the OS. OOM kills only affect the child. The parent worker continues processing.

This matters most when:

  • Tasks run untrusted or unpredictable code
  • Tasks have variable memory usage
  • You need high reliability without complex monitoring
  • You use fork-unsafe libraries (OpenTelemetry, some database drivers) that need per-task initialization via lifecycle hooks

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Run migrations once at application startup:

from pq import PQ

pq = PQ("postgresql://localhost/mydb")
pq.run_db_migrations()

This is safe to call multiple times - only pending migrations are applied.

It is also safe to call from many processes at once, for example from every worker as it starts. One process migrates at a time: it holds a Postgres advisory lock (key pq.migrations.MIGRATION_LOCK_KEY) and an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the pq tables until its transaction ends. The others wait and then find nothing to apply.

While a migration runs, the pq tables can be neither read nor written, so workers and enqueue() calls wait for it. The migration waits in turn for every transaction that already uses a pq table, and new statements on that table queue behind it. Keep transactions that touch the pq tables short during a deploy.

A call that finds the schema current takes none of these locks.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
pq creates four tables with the pq_ prefix:

Table Description pq_tasks One-off tasks pq_periodic Periodic task schedules pq_workers Running workers and their heartbeat leases pq_schema_version Alembic migration tracking

Migrate before you start workers of a new version. Workers of the previous version keep working on the migrated tables, so a rolling deploy is fine.

docs.title: Writing to the tables yourself
docs.text:
Reading the tables is safe. If your application also updates pq_tasks with its own statements, these rules hold for every row, and the database enforces them with check constraints:

Rule Constraint A RUNNING task has started_at ck_pq_tasks_running_has_started_at requeue is set only while the task is RUNNING ck_pq_tasks_requeue_only_while_running A COMPLETED or FAILED task has completed_at ck_pq_tasks_finished_has_completed_at A schedule has exactly one of run_every and cron ck_pq_periodic_interval_or_cron

The migration adds the constraints as NOT VALID: they apply to rows that are inserted or updated from then on, and the existing rows are not read. To have the old rows checked as well, run ALTER TABLE pq_tasks VALIDATE CONSTRAINT <name> for each.

These columns describe the run in progress and are cleared when it ends: worker_id, worker_claimed_at, claimed_max_runtime_seconds and, for the next version of the task, requeue. failure_kind is set on FAILED rows only. A statement of your own that moves a row to another status should clear them the way pq does.

Workers and clients of the release before these columns do not write or clear them. While some are still running, a row they finish or re-queue keeps the failure_kind it had. The orphan check is safe with them: it only acts on a worker_id written by the row's current claim.

docs.title: Alembic Integration
docs.text:
If your application uses Alembic for migrations, exclude pq tables from autogenerate to avoid conflicts:

migrations/env.py
EXCLUDED_TABLE_PREFIXES = ("pq_",)


def include_name(name: str | None, type_: str, parent_names: dict[str, str]) -> bool:
    """Filter out tables managed by external libraries."""
    if type_ == "table" and name is not None:
        return not name.startswith(EXCLUDED_TABLE_PREFIXES)
    return True


# In run_migrations_online():
context.configure(
    connection=connection,
    target_metadata=target_metadata,
    include_name=include_name,  # Add this
)

This prevents Alembic from generating migrations for pq tables, which are managed by pq.run_db_migrations().

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Runnable examples in the examples/ directory.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
examples/basic.py - Enqueue and process a task.

from pq import PQ

pq = PQ("postgresql://localhost/mydb")
pq.create_tables()

def send_email(to: str, subject: str) -> None:
    print(f"Sending email to {to}: {subject}")

pq.enqueue(send_email, to="user@example.com", subject="Hello!")
pq.run_worker_once()

docs.title: Periodic Tasks
docs.text:
examples/periodic.py - Scheduled and cron-based tasks.

from datetime import timedelta
from pq import PQ

pq = PQ("postgresql://localhost/mydb")

def heartbeat() -> None:
    print("alive")

# Run every 5 minutes
pq.schedule(heartbeat, run_every=timedelta(minutes=5))

# Run at 9am on Mondays
pq.schedule(heartbeat, cron="0 9 * * 1")

# Multiple schedules for the same function using key
def sync_data(region: str) -> None:
    print(f"Syncing {region}")

pq.schedule(sync_data, run_every=timedelta(hours=1), key="us", region="us")
pq.schedule(sync_data, run_every=timedelta(hours=2), key="eu", region="eu")

# Remove only one schedule
pq.unschedule(sync_data, key="us")

# Remove default (no key) schedule
pq.unschedule(heartbeat)

docs.title: Pausing & Resuming Periodic Tasks
docs.text:
Disable a periodic task without removing it, then re-enable it later:

from datetime import timedelta
from pq import PQ

pq = PQ("postgresql://localhost/mydb")

def sync_inventory() -> None:
    print("syncing...")

# Schedule as usual (active by default)
pq.schedule(sync_inventory, run_every=timedelta(minutes=5))

# Pause - keeps the schedule but the worker won't run it
pq.schedule(sync_inventory, run_every=timedelta(minutes=5), active=False)

# Resume
pq.schedule(sync_inventory, run_every=timedelta(minutes=5), active=True)

docs.title: Priority Queues
docs.text:
examples/priority.py - Task prioritization.

from pq import PQ, Priority

pq = PQ("postgresql://localhost/mydb")

def process(name: str) -> None:
    print(f"Processing: {name}")

# Higher priority tasks run first
pq.enqueue(process, "batch", priority=Priority.BATCH)      # 0
pq.enqueue(process, "normal", priority=Priority.NORMAL)    # 50
pq.enqueue(process, "urgent", priority=Priority.CRITICAL)  # 100

docs.title: Async Tasks
docs.text:
examples/async_tasks.py - Async handler support.

import asyncio
from pq import PQ

pq = PQ("postgresql://localhost/mydb")

async def fetch_data(url: str) -> None:
    print(f"Fetching {url}...")
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    print("Done")

pq.enqueue(fetch_data, url="https://api.example.com")
pq.run_worker_once()

docs.title: Client IDs
docs.text:
Use client_id for custom identifiers to link tasks to your domain objects.

from pq import PQ

pq = PQ("postgresql://localhost/mydb")

def process_order(order_id: int) -> None:
    print(f"Processing order {order_id}")

# Enqueue with a client-provided ID
pq.enqueue(process_order, order_id=123, client_id="order-123")

# Look up by client_id
task = pq.get_task_by_client_id("order-123")
print(f"Task status: {task.status}")

# Cancel by client_id
if task:
    pq.cancel(task.id)

# Duplicate client_id raises IntegrityError
# pq.enqueue(process_order, order_id=456, client_id="order-123")  # Error!

docs.title: Upsert
docs.text:
Use upsert() to insert or update a task by client_id. Unlike enqueue(), it won't raise on duplicates - it updates the existing task instead.

from pq import PQ

pq = PQ("postgresql://localhost/mydb")

def send_notification(user_id: int, message: str) -> None:
    print(f"Notifying user {user_id}: {message}")

# First call creates the task
pq.upsert(send_notification, user_id=42, message="Hello", client_id="notify-42")

# Second call updates the existing task (resets status to PENDING)
pq.upsert(send_notification, user_id=42, message="Updated!", client_id="notify-42")

# Useful for debouncing - only the latest version runs
for i in range(100):
    pq.upsert(send_notification, user_id=42, message=f"Message {i}", client_id="notify-42")
# Only the last message will be processed

If the task is running, the new version is queued and runs after the current run ends, so one client_id does not run twice at the same time. The run in progress is not changed. If several upserts arrive while it runs, only the last one runs next.

This makes the "continuation" pattern safe: a task can upsert its own next slice under its own client_id, and the slice starts only after the current run has ended.

from pq import PQ

DATABASE_URL = "postgresql://localhost/mydb"

def backfill(offset: int) -> None:
    more = process_rows(offset, limit=1000)
    if more:
        # Use a new client inside the task: the task runs in a forked process
        with PQ(DATABASE_URL) as client:
            client.upsert(backfill, offset=offset + 1000, client_id="backfill")

with PQ(DATABASE_URL) as pq:
    pq.upsert(backfill, offset=0, client_id="backfill")

If the worker dies while the run is in progress, the stale-task reaper re-queues the row with the waiting version instead of marking it failed. Until then (stale_task_timeout, default 1 hour) the waiting version does not run, and with the reaper disabled (stale_task_timeout=None) it never runs. Keep stale_task_timeout longer than your longest run: if the reaper picks up a run that is still alive, the waiting version can start next to it.

docs.title: Many at once
docs.text:
upsert_many() takes a list of Upsert items and applies each one as upsert() would, in one transaction. Use it for a batch: it opens one session and commits once, where a loop of upsert() calls commits once per task. If any item is invalid or a write fails, nothing is written.

from pq import PQ, Upsert

def send_notification(user_id: int, message: str) -> None:
    print(f"Notifying user {user_id}: {message}")

with PQ("postgresql://localhost/mydb") as pq:
    task_ids = pq.upsert_many(
        [
            Upsert(
                task=send_notification,
                kwargs={"user_id": user_id, "message": "Hi"},
                client_id=f"notify-{user_id}",
            )
            for user_id in [1, 2, 3]
        ]
    )

An Upsert has the same fields as the upsert() arguments: task and client_id are required, and args (a tuple), kwargs (a dict), run_at, priority and max_runtime_seconds are optional. The item does no checks of its own: upsert_many() checks each item with the same code as upsert(), so both accept the same values and raise the same errors.

  • The returned IDs are in the order of the input list.
  • A repeated client_id ends with its last version, and its ID appears once per item.
  • A RUNNING task is not changed: the new version is queued, as with upsert().

The rows are written in client_id order, so two batches that share client_ids cannot deadlock. Each row stays locked until the batch commits, and a worker that finishes one of these tasks waits for the commit. Keep batches to hundreds or a few thousand items, and split larger lists into chunks. Each chunk is then its own transaction.

docs.title: Worker Lifecycle Hooks
docs.text:
Use pre_execute and post_execute hooks to run code before/after task execution. Hooks run in the forked child process, making them ideal for fork-unsafe resources like OpenTelemetry.

from pq import PQ, Task, Periodic

pq = PQ("postgresql://localhost/mydb")

def setup_otel(task: Task | Periodic) -> None:
    """Called before task execution in forked child."""
    # Initialize tracer, create span, etc.
    print(f"[OTel] Starting span for {task.name}")

def flush_otel(task: Task | Periodic, error: Exception | None) -> None:
    """Called after task execution (success or failure)."""
    if error:
        print(f"[OTel] Recording error: {error}")
    print(f"[OTel] Flushing traces for {task.name}")

# Run worker with hooks
pq.run_worker(pre_execute=setup_otel, post_execute=flush_otel)

Hooks receive the full task object with metadata:

def pre_hook(task: Task | Periodic) -> None:
    print(f"Task ID: {task.id}")
    print(f"Task name: {task.name}")
    print(f"Client ID: {task.client_id}")
    print(f"Priority: {task.priority}")

examples/error_handling.py - Failures and cleanup.

from datetime import UTC, datetime, timedelta
from pq import PQ

pq = PQ("postgresql://localhost/mydb")

# Check failed tasks
for task in pq.list_failed():
    print(f"{task.name}: {task.error}")

# Cleanup old tasks
week_ago = datetime.now(UTC) - timedelta(days=7)
pq.clear_failed(before=week_ago)
pq.clear_completed(before=week_ago)
